blocks.x: IoT, Twin & Robotics for Automotive & Discrete Manufacturing starts at the manual inspection stations queue, pricing it honestly, then we connect machines, fleets and facilities into one operational picture, then close the loop into maintenance, scheduling and control.

The IoT, Twin & Robotics ground truth in Automotive & Discrete Manufacturing: Automotive and discrete plants chase three numbers, OEE, escapes and launch time. Sensor fabric, vision inspection and scheduling intelligence move all three simultaneously, while IATF traceability and IT/OT security raise the baseline every program must respect.

Manual inspection stations is the concrete face of a general problem: the work is shaped for a world of manual checks and batch updates, while volume and scrutiny both grew. We start with the queue, the wait and the number they produce, not with a platform license.
In Automotive & Discrete Manufacturing, where the friction concentrates:

items: Defect detection by eyes/sampling; escapes reach customers and recalls cost millions.
Body-shop and assembly sequencing by spreadsheet; changeover minutes bleed OEE.
IATF lot traceability assembled from documents; recall scoping takes days.
Legacy lines uninstrumented; OEE components and energy per unit are estimates.

blocks.x: The first two weeks belong to the baseline. manual inspection stations gets a number, an owner and a signature; the quarter belongs to a bounded slice, Line sensor fabric, live on your estate. What we promise is modest and checkable: a signed baseline, a bounded slice in production, and evidence your auditors can read without a guide. For Automotive & Discrete Manufacturing, that discipline is not optional, it is the engagement model.
Controls the auditor will ask about

Two regimes anchor the IoT, Twin & Robotics frame in Automotive & Discrete Manufacturing: IATF 16949, quality traceability evidence; IEC 62443, OT security zoning. By the time the regulator asks, the evidence already exists, that is the point of designing controls first.
